chapter_name: 003 - PART II_ OTHER WORLDS - Section 1. Of the Nature of Flatland
source_text:
Section 1.  Of the Nature of Flatland



I call our world Flatland, not because we call it so, but to make its
nature clearer to you, my happy readers, who are privileged to live in
Space.

Imagine a vast sheet of paper on which straight Lines, Triangles,
Squares, Pentagons, Hexagons, and other figures, instead of remaining
fixed in their places, move freely about, on or in the surface, but
without the power of rising above or sinking below it, very much like
shadows--only hard and with luminous edges--and you will then have a
pretty correct notion of my country and countrymen.  Alas, a few years
ago, I should have said "my universe":  but now my mind has been opened
to higher views of things.

In such a country, you will perceive at once that it is impossible that
there should be anything of what you call a "solid" kind; but I dare
say you will suppose that we could at least distinguish by sight the
Triangles, Squares, and other figures, moving about as I have described
them.  On the contrary, we could see nothing of the kind, not at least
so as to distinguish one figure from another.  Nothing was visible, nor
could be visible, to us, except Straight Lines; and the necessity of
this I will speedily demonstrate.

Place a penny on the middle of one of your tables in Space; and leaning
over it, look down upon it.  It will appear a circle.

But now, drawing back to the edge of the table, gradually lower your
eye (thus bringing yourself more and more into the condition of the
inhabitants of Flatland), and you will find the penny becoming more and
more oval to your view, and at last when you have placed your eye
exactly on the edge of the table (so that you are, as it were, actually
a Flatlander) the penny will then have ceased to appear oval at all,
and will have become, so far as you can see, a straight line.

The same thing would happen if you were to treat in the same way a
Triangle, or Square, or any other figure cut out of pasteboard.  As
soon as you look at it with your eye on the edge on the table, you will
find that it ceases to appear to you a figure, and that it becomes in
appearance a straight line.  Take for example an equilateral
Triangle--who represents with us a Tradesman of the respectable class.
Fig. 1 represents the Tradesman as you would see him while you were
bending over him from above; figs. 2 and 3 represent the Tradesman, as
you would see him if your eye were close to the level, or all but on
the level of the table; and if your eye were quite on the level of the
table (and that is how we see him in Flatland) you would see nothing
but a straight line.

When I was in Spaceland I heard that your sailors have very similar
experiences while they traverse your seas and discern some distant
island or coast lying on the horizon.  The far-off land may have bays,
forelands, angles in and out to any number and extent; yet at a
distance you see none of these (unless indeed your sun shines bright
upon them revealing the projections and retirements by means of light
and shade), nothing but a grey unbroken line upon the water.

Well, that is just what we see when one of our triangular or other
acquaintances comes toward us in Flatland.  As there is neither sun
with us, nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows, we have none
of the helps to the sight that you have in Spaceland.  If our friend
comes closer to us we see his line becomes larger; if he leaves us it
becomes smaller:  but still he looks like a straight line; be he a
Triangle, Square, Pentagon, Hexagon, Circle, what you will--a straight
Line he looks and nothing else.

You may perhaps ask how under these disadvantageous circumstances we
are able to distinguish our friends from one another: but the answer to
this very natural question will be more fitly and easily given when I
come to describe the inhabitants of Flatland.  For the present let me
defer this subject, and say a word or two about the climate and houses
in our country.

I designate our realm *Flatland* not merely as a name we use, but as a descriptor essential for clarifying its true essence to you, my fortunate readers dwelling in the boundless expanse of *Space*. Envision a vast, infinite plane—a sheet of paper where straight lines, triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, and myriad other geometric forms drift freely across the surface. Crucially, these shapes possess no ability to rise above or sink below this plane; they exist strictly within it, resembling shadows cast upon a wall, yet possessing substance, hardness, and luminous edges. This mental image offers a remarkably accurate conception of my nation and its citizens. Once, I might have termed this entire existence "my universe," but recent revelations have expanded my perspective to comprehend dimensions beyond our own.

In such a realm, it is logically impossible for anything of a "solid" nature to exist. One might reasonably assume, however, that despite this limitation, we could visually distinguish between the various figures—triangles, squares, and others—as they moved about. This assumption is fundamentally incorrect. We cannot see distinct shapes at all; rather, the only visual reality available to us consists entirely of straight lines. I shall demonstrate this necessity immediately.

Place a coin upon the center of a table in Space and lean over it to gaze downward. To your eyes, suspended above the surface, the coin appears as a perfect circle. Now, draw back to the table's edge and gradually lower your viewpoint, aligning your eye closer and closer to the tabletop. As you descend, mimicking the condition of a Flatlander, the coin transforms from a circle into an increasingly elongated oval. Finally, position your eye precisely flush against the edge of the table. At this exact moment, the coin ceases to appear oval entirely; it resolves into a simple, straight line.

The same phenomenon occurs with any shape cut from pasteboard, whether a triangle, square, or complex polygon. When viewed with the eye perfectly level with the surface, the object loses all definition of form and presents itself solely as a linear segment. Consider, for instance, an equilateral triangle, which among us signifies a tradesman of respectable standing. From a high vantage point, one perceives the full triangular geometry. As the observer lowers their gaze, the shape distorts. But when the eye rests completely on the plane—the sole mode of vision for Flatlanders—the triangle vanishes as a figure, leaving behind nothing but a straight line.

When I resided in Spaceland, I observed that your sailors encounter a striking parallel during their voyages. When gazing upon a distant island or coastline stretching along the horizon, the intricate details of bays, headlands, and indentations remain invisible. Unless illuminated sharply by your sun to create contrast through light and shadow, the landmass appears merely as a continuous, grey line upon the water. This is precisely our experience in Flatland. There is no sun here, nor any lighting mechanism capable of casting shadows to reveal depth. Consequently, when a companion approaches, regardless of whether they are a triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, or circle, they appear to us only as a straight line growing larger. As they recede, the line shrinks, yet it remains a line, devoid of angularity or curvature.

You may naturally inquire how we manage to distinguish friends from strangers under such severe visual constraints. The answer to this profound question requires a deeper understanding of our society, which I shall address when describing the inhabitants themselves. For now, permit me to briefly touch upon the climate and architecture of our unique world.
